sections.h2: How fast can an East Brunswick house actually sell?
sections.html:
An East Brunswick owner can put the house on the market, deal directly with a cash buyer, or sell privately to someone they know. Timing decides it. Marketing a house in a township this size can draw strong interest, yet it still involves staging, showings, an inspection and a lender's appraisal. A direct sale gives up some price in return for a closing date you set.

The Census Bureau estimated East Brunswick's population at 50,678 on July 1, 2025, up from 49,715 in 2020. Owners occupy eight in ten homes. Reasons people hurry include an inheritance, a rental they are done managing, or a house that needs more updating than they want to fund.

  • Agent listing: works for a house in good shape when the calendar is loose.
  • Direct cash sale: works when repairs are pending, tenants are in place, or the closing date is fixed.
  • Private sale: possible if you handle the paperwork yourself, and the township's detector certificate still applies.

sections.h2: How did East Brunswick become a commuter township?
sections.html:
East Brunswick was incorporated on February 28, 1860, carved from parts of Monroe and North Brunswick. It stayed mostly farmland until suburban building began in the 1930s, and the New Jersey Turnpike extension of 1952 set off the big surge: the population went from 5,699 in 1950 to 19,965 in 1960. The Old Bridge section in the southeast was listed as a historic district in 1977.

Geography still shapes lots and prices. East Brunswick holds 21.78 square miles of land along the Raritan River's southern shore. Lawrence Brook and Farrington Lake run along the western edge, the South River marks the east, and Manalapan Brook drains much of the south. It touches Edison, Helmetta, Milltown, Monroe, New Brunswick, North Brunswick, Old Bridge, Sayreville, South River, South Brunswick and Spotswood. Since the 2000 census, New Jersey's population center has fallen inside East Brunswick.

sections.h2: How do Route 18, the Turnpike and buses affect an East Brunswick sale?
sections.html:
Commuting drives much of the demand. The township sits at Exit 9 of the Turnpike, and Route 18 crosses its eastern half toward New Brunswick, U.S. Route 1 and the Shore. County routes 527 and 535 pass through as well, with the Garden State Parkway and Interstate 287 a short drive away in neighboring towns. Midtown Manhattan and Center City Philadelphia each take 45 to 60 minutes by car depending on traffic, and Newark Liberty International Airport is about 24 miles off.

NJ Transit's 138 goes to Port Authority in Manhattan and the 68 to Jersey City, while routes 811, 815 and 818 stay local. Suburban Transit coaches to New York depart the Transportation Center and Tower Center every 10 to 15 minutes and take 30 to 50. Road mileage totals about 206, roughly 176 of it municipal.

Census data put the typical commute at 36.5 minutes, against 30.5 statewide.

sections.h2: What business and shopping draws support East Brunswick values?
sections.html: Brunswick Square Mall, at Route 18 and Rues Lane, opened in 1970 and offers about 769,000 square feet of leasable space. Near the Turnpike and Route 18 stand the two 23-story Tower Center office towers and a 12-story Hilton, and Wipro opened its U.S. headquarters there in March 2023. At the quieter end, Giamarese Farm and Orchards has run on 35 acres of Fresh Ponds Road since 1941.

sections.h2: Which schools serve East Brunswick homes?
sections.html:
East Brunswick Public Schools operates 11 schools from pre-K to grade 12, with 8,163 students in 2024-25. Eight elementary schools cover the early grades: Bowne-Munro, Central, Chittick, Frost, Irwin, Lawrence Brook, Memorial and Warnsdorfer. Hammarskjold Upper Elementary takes grades 5 and 6, Churchill Junior High takes grades 7 to 9, and East Brunswick High School takes grades 10 to 12. Middlesex County eighth graders may also apply to the free-tuition Middlesex County Magnet Schools, one campus of which is in East Brunswick.

Confirm with the district which elementary school your street feeds before you list.

sections.h2: How expensive is East Brunswick compared with the rest of New Jersey?
sections.html:
The 2020 through 2024 survey estimates value the middle owned home at $521,900, about $67,500 over the statewide $454,400, with owners living in 80.0 percent of homes. Roughly 58 percent of adults have at least a bachelor's degree, and a third of residents were born abroad.

sections.h2: Does East Brunswick want a Certificate of Occupancy before closing?
sections.html:
No. The township's construction page says East Brunswick neither requires nor issues a Certificate of Occupancy for residential resale or rentals. A home receives its certificate when built, and later only new improvements get inspected. Questions go to Construction Inspection at 732-390-6875.

Fire safety follows its own track. Carbon monoxide alarms near bedrooms have been mandatory in one and two family homes since April 7, 2003. In 2025 the council also adopted Ordinance 25-30, which calls for smoke and carbon monoxide detector inspections and certificates when residential units are sold, leased or newly occupied. In the introduced text the fee was $50 per unit with more than 10 business days of notice before the change of occupant, $75 at 4 to 10 days, and $125 under 4, plus $20 for a re-inspection after a failure. Ask the township for today's schedule and book early, since the late fee is the highest.

sections.h2: What will an East Brunswick seller pay at closing?
sections.html:
State law puts the realty transfer fee on the seller. Running the state's tiers against $521,900, the Census figure for a middle-priced owned home here, gives roughly $4,385, and a price above $1,000,000 adds a graduated percentage charge.

  • Transfer fee: collected from the seller at filing, using a tiered rate per $500 of price.
  • Detector certificate: a township charge that climbs as the closing date nears.
  • Payoffs: your mortgage and any liens come out of the proceeds.
  • Tax form: a GIT/REP certification travels with the deed and decides whether a nonresident seller must prepay.

sections.h2: Which office files the deed on an East Brunswick sale?
sections.html: The Middlesex County Clerk handles it, at the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, in New Brunswick. Weekday hours end at 4:10, but the office asks that you arrive by 4. The registry's number is 732-745-3002. Its posted schedule lists $45 for a deed's first page and $10 for each page after that, with a $6 name fee in some cases. A free Property Alert service emails you when a filed document matches your property.

sections.h2: What if my East Brunswick house has been a short-term rental?
sections.html: Chapter 182 of the township code governs short-term rentals, and the council amended it through Ordinance 25-34 in 2025. If you hosted guests, read the current chapter or call the township before describing the house's rental history to a buyer.

faqs.q: Is a resale inspection mandatory in East Brunswick?
faqs.a: No Certificate of Occupancy is needed for a residential resale. A 2025 ordinance does call for smoke and carbon monoxide detector certification on sale, so ask the township how to book it.

faqs.q: What sets the timeline for a cash closing in East Brunswick?
faqs.a: The contract does. With no lender appraisal involved, the pace depends mainly on the title search, the detector certificate, and the deed filing with the Middlesex County Clerk.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee on an East Brunswick sale mine or the buyer's?
faqs.a: It is the seller's. A $521,900 price, the Census figure for the middle owned home, produces about $4,385 under the state schedule.

faqs.q: Where is the deed filed after closing here?
faqs.a: With the Middlesex County Clerk, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick, through the registry at 732-745-3002.

faqs.q: Can a house with tenants still be sold in East Brunswick?
faqs.a: Yes. The ordinance reaches sales, leases and other occupancy, so time the detector inspection around the tenants' move-out or the closing.
